title: PlayAgain: a direct neural interface with a paediatric neuroorthosis to restore grasping in children with a paralysed hand
summary:
Grasping is a basic daily movement used in tasks like eating, drawing, and playing. Injuries, diseases and surgical procedures such as spinal cord injuries, strokes, cerebral palsy or hemispherotomy can limit these activities. 
Restoring grasping function with training and powered exoskeletons can be a great help in daily activities and thus improve quality of life of affected patients. Children in particular can benefit from the brain's neuroplasticity, i.e., its ability to change and adapt, as this is more pronounced in childhood than in adulthood. Constantly repeating movements can strengthen existing neurological pathways and support the formation of new connections, which may eventually lead to a restoration of hand function. However, the availability of a rehabilitative system, which include real time neurofeedback and intuitive control of an exoskeleton for children is severely limited. Research and development of solutions is concentrated on adults.
For this reason, the PlayAgain study aims to develop a direct neural interface with an exergame and a pediatric neuroorthosis to restore grasping in children with a paralyzed hand and also focus on reducing muscle atrophy, which is important for improving quality of life.
A key aspect of our approach involves training the children to interact with our rehabilitation environment. By doing so, we aim to enable them to intuitively and proportionally control a virtual and mechatronics systems.
conditions: Paresis of the hand due to all causes, particularly in cases of paraplegia, hemiparesis of various origins including after hemispherotomy, hemorrhage, stroke, or inflammatory diseases of the central nervous system.

interventions.name:
The study includes two intervention areas within the same cohort: the hand orthosis and the rehabilitation game. These are designed to assess, train, and improve residual motor functions over time.

Inclusion criteria:
Neurological disorders presenting with hand paresis
Exclusion criteria:
Age < 3 years
No detectable muscle activity
Intractable spasticity
Open injuries
Drug or alcohol use
Lack of ability to cooperate
Severe psychiatric disorders
